title: The community council: governing and caring for Lviv’s Jews
summary: The council’s work shows how communal authority handled practical needs, public representation, and welfare.

## A community that had to govern

In Lviv—called Lwów in Polish, Lemberg in German, and Lvov in Russian—the Jewish community was more than a congregation. Its leaders managed communal funds, collected and allocated revenue, oversaw religious and civic institutions, and tried to meet the practical needs of residents. The memorial book presents this work across very different political eras: from a community hospital established in 1801, through nineteenth-century disputes over taxation and welfare, to the crisis of Nazi occupation. These administrations should not be mistaken for one continuous body with unchanged authority. Each operated under different rulers and conditions.

The book’s records distinguish the historic community administration from a later “Jewish Council.” That distinction matters. A prewar or nineteenth-century communal committee, even when it levied taxes or argued with authorities, was not the same institution as a council imposed under Nazi rule. The U.S. Holocaust Memorial Museum explains that German occupation authorities established Jewish councils to enforce orders, while council members also tried to maintain basic services under coercion. In Lviv, Joseph Parnes was killed after refusing to hand over Jews for forced labor. The wartime council’s constrained and dangerous position was therefore fundamentally different from ordinary communal governance. ([USHMM, “Jewish Councils (Judenraete)”](https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/jewish-councils-judenraete))

## Revenue, responsibility, and contention

The memorial book’s account of the [Lviv Jewish Community]( /communities/lviv/records/mention_29f3b3d83123a195db32ef3d) describes representatives, officials, taxation, and proposed welfare institutions. It also names people who took part in or led communal affairs. [Shmuel Di-Horowitz](/communities/lviv/records/mention_031df3805489cb2233911ac1) and [Dr. Yaakov Diamond](/communities/lviv/records/mention_a84360be88424f03e61c4023) were elected to the community council in 1898. The book also names [Pinhas Ditersdorf](/communities/lviv/records/mention_715315767e4b8d179a452227), a community scribe dismissed during an investigation. These brief references show how administration depended not only on prominent elected representatives, but also on clerks and other staff—and how internal disputes could reach into their working lives.

Taxation was tied to the community’s capacity to provide. The English translation of the memorial book describes revenue from kosher meat taxes, leases, donations, and legacies supporting institutions and communal expenses. Those arrangements could provoke disagreement over who controlled the proceeds and how they should be used. [David-Hirsch Sokal](/communities/lviv/records/mention_32e74ad83ba68ddb015c674b) is remembered as managing hospital affairs with Lib Sternklahr and opposing tax lessees. The book also names [Lev Sternklahr](/communities/lviv/records/mention_b1a0ed053935db8c371450fe) and [Meir Yerachmiel Mizem](/communities/lviv/records/mention_a3078066c4c7920c66ec7356) among committee members. Taken together, these names place institutional care inside a world of administration, bargaining, and sometimes conflict—not outside it.

A separate passage records a bribery case involving [Jacob-Aharon](/communities/lviv/records/mention_05423dab7512a9e020ab4118), a council member, and [Meir Hershel](/communities/lviv/records/mention_c37a5674f47e494ca3e3dd18), a council clerk. The account says both were fined and removed from their positions. The record identifies the body as a “Jewish Council,” but the supplied evidence does not establish enough chronology here to equate it with the Nazi-era Judenrat. The safest reading is to preserve the book’s terminology while keeping this episode distinct from the occupation councils discussed by the USHMM.

## A hospital sustained by communal resources

The hospital gives the clearest long view of the community’s caring role. The memorial book says the community maintained a Jewish hospital from 1801. It describes a system with a doctor, surgeons, a midwife, and other medical workers, and notes that the institution’s management was appointed by the community. Its expenses were supported through bathhouse leases and contributions from tax lessees and individuals. ([Memorial book, hospital and community history](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/lviv/lvi197.html))

The book’s later account says the hospital fell into severe decline and was reorganized by the community committee. [Jacob Mendel Shitz](/communities/lviv/records/mention_da89b6de5ef0406a920caef5) is named in connection with the hospital. The record set does not supply a precise date for this reorganization, so it should not be folded into the 1801 founding as though both were one event. The institution’s history instead suggests repeated work: securing income, maintaining services, and adapting care as the community and its resources changed.

The wider history adds scale. The memorial book’s English translation reports that the hospital treated many patients in the nineteenth century and that, in 1902, it was enlarged with support from Maurycy Lazarus, who funded a modern hospital building that was handed to the Jewish community. It also describes other institutions, including an orphanage and a home for incurable patients. ([Memorial book, hospital and welfare institutions](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/lviv/lvi303.html)) These details are the book’s account, not independent confirmation. A further research path would be the **Lazarus hospital on Rappaporta Street**, whose later wartime seizure is also mentioned in the memorial book.

## Relief beyond the hospital

Care also meant food, education, and aid to people without reliable income. The book dates the founding of Lviv’s first soup kitchen to 1874, naming Rabbi Löwenstein as its chairman and Dr. J. Fried as deputy. Its account of the community’s wider nineteenth-century work includes support for schools, children, orphans, and charitable associations. The variety of these activities helps explain why budgets and taxation mattered: communal leaders were trying to sustain more than one institution at a time. ([Memorial book, community welfare and the soup kitchen](https://www.jewishgen.org/Yizkor/lviv/lvi303.html))

This work did not happen without debate. The book records conflict over how far the committee should shape religious education, with Orthodox opponents resisting intervention in cheders and Talmud Torah schools. The tension illustrates a persistent challenge: a community council might collect and distribute funds for shared needs, yet its decisions could touch religious practice and the authority of different groups. The same committee could be expected to provide public services while remaining answerable to a diverse community.

## Changing administrations, changing dangers

The book also mentions a [Rescue Committee](/communities/lviv/records/mention_83faf16b072ff0d334e2b8af) during the Russian occupation of Lviv, and says its operations were transferred to the community. The supplied summary does not specify when the transfer occurred or precisely what work was involved. That gap matters: rescue activity during an occupation should not be described as routine welfare administration, nor should its timing or reach be inferred from the short reference alone.

By the Second World War, Lviv’s Jewish population was large and internally diverse. The USHMM describes interwar Lwów as a major Jewish center, with Jews making up about a third of the city’s population before the war and participating in varied religious, political, and social organizations. ([USHMM, “The Diverse Jewish Community of Interwar Lwów”](https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/gallery/the-diverse-jewish-community-of-interwar-lwow-poland-now-lviv-ukraine)) Under Nazi occupation, however, institutions of care faced confiscation, starvation, deportation, and murder. The memorial book recalls that the Jewish hospital was seized and that welfare workers could help only a few people amid mass deprivation. Its testimony preserves the limits of communal care when the governing power was organized to destroy the community. ([Memorial book, wartime Lviv](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/lviv/lvi593.html))

The community council’s story is thus not simply a story of offices or budgets. It is a history of people trying to turn collective resources into treatment, food, education, and assistance—and of the sharp boundary between imperfect but locally organized communal government and coercive rule under occupation. The names of committee members, hospital managers, clerks, and relief organizers keep that work human, while the changing political context explains why the same words—“community” and “council”—could describe institutions with radically different powers and purposes.
